Pele Yoetz 132:7: And a great story is known that happened to a certain great man who was inclined to die, and suddenly he was aroused and strengthened and sat up on the bed and asked for tefillin to put on, and from then on he recovered until he returned to health. And he revealed his secret: that while he was fainting in his illness, he saw that they were weighing his merits and his sins against each other, and the scales were even, and therefore he rose and was aroused and tipped the scale of merit, and he lived from his illness. Therefore, this is the time to perform mitzvot at the time of illness with all one's mustered strength, and let his righteousness go before him, for charity saves from death, and let him pour out his speech, seeking forgiveness, day by day, for the prayer of the sick person for himself is pleasing, as they said (Bereishit Rabbah 53:14), on the verse "and God heard the voice of the lad" (Genesis 21:17).
Pele Yoetz 132:8: Indeed, remembered for good, the crown of my head, my father and teacher, of blessed memory, for the life of the World to Come - for every day of his illness (that one) he would say "you have sought me, my desire is toward you," and the other confessions and supplications of Yom Kippur, and streams of water would flow from his eyes - happy is the eye that saw these things. And to whoever came to visit him, he would say, "see the end of flesh and blood" - an eye that saw and blessed him, happy is he and happy is his portion. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already said (Berachot 8a): for this let every pious man pray, "to You, at a time of finding" (Psalms 32:6) - this refers to death - for then it is a time of favor, the fitting time to strive with great vigor and might to repent and to command his sons and his household after him, "and they shall keep the way of the LORD," for then his words are heeded, and the sons keep their father's command more than they keep the Ten Commandments, and the merit of his sons depends on him, and it is a time to have mercy on his own soul, his own spirit, and his own soul - for if not now, when?
Pele Yoetz 132:9: And a person should not worry about frightening the members of his household lest they see him occupying himself with matters of death and be terrified, for this is vanity and vexation of spirit, for these things do not kill but rather give life to the dead - and all such things are fitting to do while one is still young, for a person does not know his own time, as the Tanna said (Shabbat 153a): repent one day before your death - all the more so when he has fallen ill, for then "no judgment need tarry" (Berachot 40a[?]), and whoever is alert profits greatly. And when he recovers from his illness, he shall not forget all the days of his life that he reached the gates of death, and through the LORD's compassion upon him He gave him life, and he shall not return again to folly, but shall walk in the way of the good and keep the paths of the righteous.
Pele Yoetz 133:1: Kindness - Kindness is the pillar of the world, to the point that it is said (Psalms 89:3), "the world is built with kindness." And it is one of the things whose fruits one enjoys in this world while the principal remains for the World to Come. And the general principle of kindness is that one perform kindness with his body, his money, and his words, and every man shall do whatever is in his power to do - there is no distinction between much and little, for he fulfills a Torah-mandated mitzvah - such as opening the door for one who knocks, or exchanging money into small coins, or handing something to his fellow, and the like. How many things there are that are easy to perform as acts of kindness, to the point that one person almost benefits while the other loses nothing at all, and yet people treat them with contempt and do not know what kindness is and how great is its goodness. And it is astonishing about people who give much money for the mitzvah of opening the ark, or for carrying the Torah scroll, and the like, or to be a sandak, and the like - things that are neither Torah-mandated nor Rabbinic, but merely a cherishing of a mitzvah and a custom of Israel - while regarding Torah-mandated mitzvot that they could perform easily and without money and without cost, such as the mitzvah of acts of kindness, and the mitzvah of honoring father and mother, and the mitzvah of "you shall rise before gray hair and honor the presence of an elder," and the like - so many such mitzvot they transgress with disregard, without setting their heart to fulfilling them, which are mitzvot to be fulfilled - may the good LORD atone for this.
Pele Yoetz 133:2: And included in the mitzvah of acts of kindness is the mitzvah of "and you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18) - that he picture in his mind, if he himself needed that thing, how he would wish his fellow to do for him, so shall he do for his fellow. And he should not worry about the trouble to his own body, for "according to the pain is the reward." And the man whom the LORD has graced with wealth in this regard shall glory in his wealth by doing justice and charity and gracious and kind loans, and happy is the man who does this: that he set aside a tenth of his money, or some portion of his possessions, for gracious and kind loans, and also buy household items needed by the many and lend them out - of him Scripture says (Psalms 112:3), "wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever; his horn shall be exalted in honor" - in this world and in the World to Come. And a person can cheaply purchase the life of the World to Come - such as, if he buys a plasterer's pole and other tools of craft to lend to others, he shall carry blessings from the borrower, and the LORD shall command the blessing be with him. And now, because of our sins, there are many like the Egyptian midwives among the Hebrew women, and a woman whose eye is stingy, and they make disputes, refusing to lend trivial things. Whoever desires kindness shall teach his daughter to be a woman of kindness and a woman of charity, and let her not turn away the poor disgraced, nor turn him away empty, and the LORD shall repay sevenfold into their bosom, and they shall eat their allotted portion.
Pele Yoetz 133:3: However, an obligation rests upon the recipient of kindness not to lock the door before people of kindness - such as, by being a wicked borrower who does not repay, or by borrowing an item and not being exacting to return it to its owner quickly and in the manner it was given to him, and similar evils that cause the door to be locked and cause regret over past kindnesses. And who is like the wise man who sees the consequences, and regarding every matter of mitzvah sets his heart to think and be careful not to come to cause regret over past kindnesses, and also not to come to transgress "before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14). And where there is concern about cheats, he should not be a guarantor for his fellow or his brother, and should not lend to them except against a pledge and with a document, and the like, in a manner that performing the mitzvah shall be sweet and pleasant to him and he can persist in it. Of this it is said (Psalms 112:5-6), "good is the man who is gracious and lends, he manages his affairs with judgment, for he shall never be moved; the righteous man shall be for an everlasting remembrance." Also, "he who eats his money" [pursues his own gain relentlessly] shall withdraw his hand from doing good and from lending to a poor man in his time of need even without a pledge, knowing that he has nothing to pledge - for he shall know with certainty that "whoever lends to the LORD is gracious to the poor" (Proverbs 19:17), and without any doubt the LORD shall repay him principal and profit, increasing good measure in this world and in the World to Come, and he shall not come to regret past kindnesses, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 133:4: And included in acts of kindness is the great mitzvah of hospitality, which is greater than receiving the presence of the Shechinah and rising early for the study house, as they said in the Talmud (Shabbat 127a). And it is true that it is very burdensome, especially when the guests are numerous and there are small children, so that confusion increases and they stay for many days, and the household's expenses increase and the trouble increases, and the nearby inclination causes one to grow weary of the mitzvah. However, the complete man shall make a reckoning and weigh his loss against the reward of the mitzvah, and according to the pain, so does he give peace of mind to his Former, so that his reward grows, and man is born to toil - happy is he whose toil is for the sake of Torah and mitzvot and gives peace of mind to his Former; he grows in a good name and departs with a good name. And included in this is the great mitzvah of "and you shall love your fellow as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18): that he clothe himself in his fellow's garment, imagining how he himself would wish to be shown mercy.
Pele Yoetz 133:5: However, an obligation rests upon the guest not to burden the host, and this is a matter requiring understanding, to recognize a person by his traits and get to the bottom of his mind, and not to do anything against his will - I have already written a bit of this above under the entry "Derech Eretz" [proper conduct]. And especially if the guest suspects that the host is evil-eyed and stingy of eye, that when he eats and drinks he says so but his heart is not with it, let him flee from him and distance himself from him, for he enters into a category of robbery. And they also said in the Holy Zohar that it would be better for a person to strangle himself than to eat the bread of one with an evil eye. And every person must be concerned about this, and let him do whatever is in his power to do to minimize his stay at the host's home as much as possible, and let him too contribute what he can toward the household expenses from time to time.
Pele Yoetz 133:6: And if this is not possible, let him repay him with thanks by blessing him, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, instituted (Berachot 46a) the blessing of the guest, that he bless the host in the Grace after Meals every time he eats at his home, and let his mouth be full of his praise, and similar words that settle the heart of the host and the members of his household when he opens with the honor of hospitality, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, would do, for they all opened with the honor of hospitality, as brought in the Talmud (Berachot 63a), in a manner that they should know how good is their portion and how pleasant their lot, and how much good is stored up for them in this world and the next, until they receive them with joy and a pleasant countenance, and the trouble and expense shall be light in their eyes according to the greatness of the good. And the man who is compelled to be a guest in the host's home for many days should not let his heart be grieved, for these are wonders of one of perfect understanding and to Him deeds are accounted, and the host and the guest do the will of their Maker, for so did the King, the King of the universe, establish His kingdom.
Pele Yoetz 133:7: And the essence of the kindness one performs with his fellow is that he perform kindness with his fellow's soul, and strive to bring him merit and teach him and guide him on the straight path he should walk, and rebuke him to his face - and if he rebukes him with strikes for his iniquity, so that it be an atonement for him, and rescue him from the judgment of Heaven, this too is a kindness greater than one performed with a smiling face. And it is included in this that he strive with all his strength to bring rest to the soul [of the deceased] - such as praying for him after his death, that he have proper rest. And since he cannot do this for every single one of Israel, he should not refrain from saying, from time to time, a general prayer for all the souls of Israel, and give charity for their rest. And let him strive for the children of Israel, to raise them upon the Torah as much as he can bear, for then they save their father from the province of Gehinnom, and there is no kindness greater than this. And likewise, when he studies the words of the Sages and carries their names on his lips, let him intend that their lips move in the grave, for this too is a great kindness.
Pele Yoetz 133:8: And everything said in this matter, the obligation to perform kindness grows greater regarding one's parents and one's own offspring and one's relatives - the nearer relative takes precedence, in the manner they said, "your own poor take precedence," and so on (Bava Metzia 71a), and "do not hide yourself from your own flesh" (Isaiah 58:7). And more and more does the obligation grow to perform kindness with oneself and one's own body - "he who repays his own soul is a man of kindness" (Proverbs 11:17). And as they said (Yalkut Shimoni, Proverbs, remez 947) about Hillel the Elder, that when he would go to eat, he would say, "I go to perform kindness with the guest I have," meaning his own soul, as it is written (ibid.), "he who repays his own soul is a man of kindness." And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, "your own life takes precedence" (Bava Metzia 62a). In a manner that the mitzvah of performing kindness is a garland of grace for all worldly matters, and all the more so for all the mitzvot of the Torah. And if he sets his mind and directs his heart to this, certainly the Holy One, blessed be He, establishes for him a reward for the kindness, for if he does anything at all that gives peace of mind to his own Maker, behold, he performs kindness with Him.
Pele Yoetz 133:9: And also, if he increases the honor of his house - that is, his wife - this is kindness, and all the more so since these matters are ancient. And especially if he is a righteous man, for regarding such a case they told in the Talmud (Gittin 68b) that they proclaim in heaven that whoever gives her peace of mind merits the World to Come - provided there is no hint of prohibition, for then he shall nullify others' will before the will of his Maker. But in any case, there is a time for every desire, and there is a time when it is fitting for a man to strive to give her peace of mind. And sometimes the neglect of Torah is itself its fulfillment, according to the time, the place, the season, and what kind of person one is.
Pele Yoetz 133:10: And if he brings merit to his fellow or rebukes him for his iniquity, he performs an act of kindness, and likewise regarding all mitzvot between man and his fellow. It is included in acts of kindness toward himself and his own flesh if he indulges and enjoys this world - for since his soul desires it, he performs an act of kindness, provided he directs his heart to Heaven and blesses properly and does not indulge more than is fitting. And all the more so if he performs mitzvot and good deeds, or brings merit to the many - this is performing kindness with his own soul and with the soul of his father and mother, and performing kindness with the Holy One, blessed be He, and with all Israel, and with all the upper and lower worlds. And above all, his reward is with him and his recompense is before him, besides the mitzvah itself - it is only right that he receive his reward for his kindness and his truth. And knowledge of opposites is one and the same, so let the man tremble and be seized, for every transgression he commits shall surely be punished also for causing evil to all the worlds and for the distress of the upper and lower realms. Therefore the God-fearing man shall choose to perform kindness and receive good reward from the faithful God, who keeps covenant and kindness, and with the measure a person measures, it is measured to him (Megillah 12b, Sotah 8b), and He who is abundant in kindness tends toward kindness (Rosh Hashanah 17a). And just as the Holy One, blessed be He, does not repay him according to his own deeds but performs kindness and a free gift with him, so shall he perform kindness with every person - even if he is his enemy who has repaid him evil, he shall not take revenge and shall not bear a grudge and shall not withhold good, and the LORD shall not withhold good. And if the kindness performed for an individual is great, all the more so shall the one who removes a stumbling block from the path of the many, or performs public needs, have his reward grow according to the greatness of the good, and according to how many benefit from it, so does he receive reward for it.
Pele Yoetz 134:1: Suspicion - Suspicion is a transgression that many stumble into, thinking there is no sin in it - as Maimonides, of blessed memory, wrote (Hilchot Teshuvah 4:4), that since it is not counted for him as an iniquity, there is no presumption he shall repent of it. And furthermore, it is a spirit within a person, and a person is not master over his spirit to restrain the spirit so that he not become suspicious - but in any case, it is in a person's power to guard his mouth and his tongue and not let it be heard from his mouth that he suspects some person, for it causes great evil - disgrace, division, hatred, and rivalry, until the flame rises high. And if he wishes to search after a theft, let him search among all the members of the group, treating "the righteous like the wicked," and then none of them shall have a complaint. And likewise, every clever person should act with knowledge in a manner that the thief not come to disgrace, for they said (Sotah 10b): better that a person cast himself into a fiery furnace than shame his fellow publicly. All the more so for the sake of a monetary loss, one should not shame his fellow publicly, for it is like shedding blood. And whoever shames another shall be covered with shame, for he commits a greater transgression than the thief - for the thief transgresses only a negative commandment and need only pay, but whoever shames his fellow publicly has no portion in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 134:2: Behold, therefore, if something is stolen from a man, let him consider the end of the matter from its beginning and not add loss to his loss, and "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles" (Proverbs 21:23). And the man who desires life shall muster his strength to master his own spirit so as not to suspect at all, but shall say: who knows, perhaps something happened to me that I do not now recall, for many times it is so found, and it has happened that the theft is found in the possession of a gentile who had not been suspected, and sometimes it is kept safe in his own hand without his knowledge, and after some time it is found. And if he suspected some person and had a quarrel with him, where shall he take his disgrace? At the very least, let him greatly appease him and humble himself before him to seek his forgiveness. And likewise in every matter, he should not judge by the appearance of his eyes and find fault in a person, for as he has done, so shall be done to him - and whoever judges favorably is judged favorably from Heaven, for although the Omnipresent knows the truth of matters, in any case, according to His own measures, if He judges unfavorably, He judges him for having done something that leans toward the unfavorable side and for the unfavorable aspect that is in that matter; and if He judges favorably, whenever there is a favorable aspect in that matter he did, "He has not beheld iniquity and has not seen mischief." And great is a transgression for its own sake (Horayot 10b). And although we find that there is punishment for a transgression for its own sake, as Aaron was punished for making the calf (Vayikra Rabbah 10:4), according to his own greatness he was punished - this appears to my humble opinion at present, and examine it carefully.
Pele Yoetz 134:3: However, just as there is a prohibition against a person suspecting the innocent, so there is a prohibition against bringing oneself into suspicion, for he transgresses "before the blind you shall not place a stumbling block" (Leviticus 19:14). All the more so is it fitting for a person to guard himself and his money and distance himself from every person as a robber, so as not to come into suspicion. And even if he comes to perform a mitzvah, it is fitting to consider whether, because of this, the multitude of the people will come to speak disparagingly - let him refrain, for it is possible that against the harm caused to several people who might sin, the mitzvah he performs is not worth it. And everything depends on the obligation of the mitzvah - a scale and just balances shall be in his hand to know what to do and what to refrain from. All the more so shall he distance himself greatly from anything resembling ugliness. And now there are many ignorant people who say, "what does it matter to me? Let my portion be with whoever is suspected - it is a merit for me, and he shall bear his own iniquity." If only they were wise, they would understand that he takes a leading share for having transgressed "before the blind."
Pele Yoetz 134:4: And it is fitting for whoever is suspected to enter into the thickness of the matter to remove himself from suspicion, for how many decrees did our Rabbis, of blessed memory, decree, forbidding the permitted because of appearance and because of suspicion, and they said in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 35b) that the Rabbis imposed an oath upon the hired worker, even though he was not obligated to swear, but rather to put the employer's mind at ease. From this let the wise man hear that even one who is careful not to let an oath come from his own mouth should not refrain from swearing in a place of suspicion, in order to clear himself and remove himself from suspicion, and let his deeds be pure and upright in the eyes of all who see him, and fulfill what the Torah said (Numbers 32:22), "and you shall be clear before the LORD and before Israel" - and through this he shall find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 135:1: Piety - It is fitting for every person to conduct himself with piety and do whatever is in his power to do, for just as regarding money, "he who loves money shall not be satisfied with money" (Ecclesiastes 5:9), and even though he has enough for his own need, his eye is not satisfied and half his desire is not in his hand - all the more so should this be so regarding giving peace of mind to his Former and gaining one hour of tranquility of spirit in the World to Come, which is better than all the life of this world. And whoever has the means to perform matters of piety, and holds fast, saying, "it is enough for me to perform the obligation that cannot be dispensed with otherwise" - I am concerned that he is among those who do not have regard for the honor of their Maker, who would have been better off not born (Chagigah 11b), for since he could have honored the LORD and given peace of mind to his Former by performing these matters of piety, and he did not do so, it turns out that he does not have regard for the honor of his Maker. And furthermore, with the measure a person measures, it is measured to him, and if he acts beyond the letter of the law, the Holy One, blessed be He, deals with him beyond the strict letter of the law - and woe, who could survive if the Holy One, blessed be He, judged him according to strict law?
Pele Yoetz 135:2: Behold, therefore, an obligation rests upon a person to perform all matters of piety according to the Holy Zohar and the Ari, of blessed memory, for he builds his chambers in heaven and gives peace of mind to his Former. And the man who loves the LORD with a fierce love, as is fitting, shall not find anything too difficult for him to do, for those who truly love the LORD say, "would that our death give peace of mind to our Former," as it is written (Song of Songs 1:3), "therefore they love You even unto death."
Pele Yoetz 135:3: And all the more so in matters that depend on a dispute, even where the ruling has become established and the world follows the lenient opinion, it is fitting and proper for those who fear the Name and love it to satisfy every doubt and satisfy every opinion, and to be concerned lest the law be with the one who is stringent - as in the parable of the physician that I wrote above under the entry "Zehirut" [caution] - see there. (And I already have plans to arrange, in a separate pamphlet, all matters of piety and matters of dispute, how it is fitting to act to satisfy all views - may the LORD complete this for me and help me complete the work.)
Pele Yoetz 135:4: However, all these measures were said only for those who keep them private (Shabbat 76b), and if regarding all matters it is written (Micah 6:8), "and walk humbly with your God," all the more so regarding matters of piety, for not everyone who wishes to take the Name may take it. And there is a person who thinks he is performing a mitzvah and piety, and, showing off his humility, appears arrogant, giving room for sin and for people to speak disparagingly of him. And everything depends on what kind of person he is, and on the place, and on the matter - sometimes the neglect of Torah is itself its fulfillment. And how good and how pleasant it is to fulfill the saying of the sweet singer of Israel, "I shall walk within my house with the integrity of my heart" (Psalms 101:2). And this is a great principle in all matters of piety and fear of Heaven: that whenever he can fulfill a good thing, he shall fulfill it, and whatever he can do, he shall do, and these do not preclude one another - and through this he shall receive good reward for what he did not do due to some cause, as though he had done it.
Pele Yoetz 136:1: One's Father-in-Law and Mother-in-Law - Well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Midrash Tehillim 7:4; Mechilta, Yitro 18:7; Masechet Amalek 21), that a person is obligated in the honor of his father-in-law and mother-in-law. And behold, every person is careful about this because they entice him with words, as one does regarding one's own mother. But the essence of the honor is to honor them at their death, giving them peace of mind, just as one does for one's own father and mother, and especially if they have no sons - who shall care for them besides him? And it is fitting to care for them, honoring them all the more in their life and at their death, and through this they shall be comforted for not having sons, and shall give thanks for their portion. And when the sons-in-law are good, then daughters are preferable to sons for them. And there is reason to say that the obligation of honor owed to one's father-in-law and mother-in-law is even greater, for through them he is saved from sin and merits to be built up. And how many good qualities does a man and woman have who have merited this! And how much labor and how much trouble the father-in-law and mother-in-law took until they raised the daughter and until they married her to him - it was as hard as iron for them, and how shall he repay them? An obligation rests upon the groom not to be ungrateful, and to be like a son to them.
Pele Yoetz 136:2: And it is especially necessary to urge the wife to be careful and alert regarding the honor of her father-in-law and mother-in-law, for they said (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 26): "honor your father," and adjacent to it, "you shall not commit adultery" - what is the connection between this and that? To teach you that if a man marries a wife and she does not honor his father and mother in their old age, it is as though he committed adultery all his days - therefore it is said, "honor," and "you shall not commit adultery." And how much labor a person labors and how much great pain he suffers with his children until he brings them to the age of marriage, hoping for good, to marry them off and find rest for his soul - and afterward the daughter-in-law rises up against her mother-in-law, and dispute and quarrel increase in the house, and this causes the son too to make dispute and quarrel with his father and mother, for it is a man's way to be attached to his wife, and "a constant dripping is a driving quarrel of a wife" (Proverbs 19:13), and in the end the sons separate from their father's table, and even brothers separate from each other because of the evil of quarrel and dispute among the wives, and it turns out that "father and mother" fulfilled in them (Jeremiah 14:19), "we hoped for peace, but no good came; and for a time of healing, and behold, terror." And that woman shall bear her own iniquity and the iniquity of her husband, and evil shall come upon her, and bitter shall be her end - as she has done, so shall her own daughters-in-law do to her, besides her punishment reserved for her in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 136:3: And "a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised" (Proverbs 31:30) - that she honor her father-in-law and mother-in-law even more than her own husband, as a king and queen, and her entire aim shall be to attain and know their will and to do their will according to their own wish, and she shall not do any matter, small or great, without their permission. And it goes without saying when the son is dependent on his father's table, eating his bread, that this is part of the affection for their honor - but even if the son supports his father and mother, he should not, on this account, treat their honor lightly, God forbid, even if it is burdensome to him, for the sons' merit is from their fathers' support, and their righteousness stands forever. And well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Kiddushin 31b; Yerushalmi Peah 1:1; see Yerushalmi Kiddushin 1:7) that there is one who feeds his father and mother fattened birds and inherits Gehinnom, and there is one who makes them grind at the millstone and inherits the Garden of Eden - and everything depends on pleasant speech and conducting oneself with honor toward them. And even if her father-in-law and mother-in-law are burdensome and their traits are harsh, as is the custom of many elders, a man and woman who are sensible and God-fearing shall bear it and not wear out, and shall not oppose them, God forbid, and shall be in awe of them because of the day of judgment, for God shall bring into judgment every evil word and every kind of contempt. And whoever honors them shall be honored, and his reward shall be doubled and redoubled - according to the pain is the reward.
Pele Yoetz 136:4: And this mitzvah rests upon the husband, to guide his wife and instruct her with all firmness that she bear and be exceedingly careful regarding the honor of his father and mother. And if he sees that she treats their honor lightly, even if it seems to him that the law is on her side, in any case, in their presence he shall rebuke her and silence her with a reproach, in order to put his father's and mother's minds at ease, and in private he shall appease her with good words for the sake of domestic peace. But it is known that wisdom is with the aged, and understanding should always come from elders - therefore, if it happens that the son's wife is a bad, hard-spirited woman, an obligation rests upon the elders to bear with her and guide her gently and pleasantly, and not to burden her, and if she does things improperly, they shall discipline her between themselves and her privately and shall not reveal her disgrace to people, but shall rather praise her and hold her in esteem before people. All the more so shall they not reveal it and make a quarrel with her father and mother, and all the more so, a fortiori, shall they guard their own souls not to reveal her disgrace to her husband, lest resentment enter his heart and he come to hate her. And woe to a father and mother if they cause this, for the holy Name, written in holiness, the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded to be erased upon the water in order to make peace between a man and his wife (Shabbat 116a). And it is far better for father and mother to bear a thousand evils than to place division between a man and his wife.
Pele Yoetz 136:5: Therefore, father and mother need great understanding to conduct themselves with good conduct toward their sons and daughters-in-law, so that their match turn out well, in peace and uprightness. And even if there is some friction and dispute between them, they shall be very careful that their words not become known outside, in the public eye, for this is folly and shame for both sides and causes evil speech and a bad name for their souls. And I have already stated that if they cannot restrain their own spirit to be in peace and uprightness, it is good and right that they not dwell together, and separation is beneficial for them - this is their life.
Pele Yoetz 137:1: Chametz - The mitzvah of removing chametz [leavened bread] is great, for the commentators have written that the plain meaning of this mitzvah is the allusion within it, that it is to remove the unclean spirit and the evil inclination from within us - therefore, whoever increases in searching is praiseworthy. And the essence of this mitzvah rests upon the women, to clean the houses very well and to search after chametz in cracks and crevices, in places of concern and places without concern, and to scald all vessels, even those used only with cold food, and to sort and clean the wheat well - and such caution and good customs, all of them the custom of the early sages, are beloved, and all have a root above, and "our handiwork He has established" to remove the unclean spirit. And therefore the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote that he was very careful regarding the prohibition of chametz, and whoever is stringent with himself in extra stringencies is assured that he shall not sin the entire year, for since he has removed the unclean spirit entirely and given no room for the Other Side to have dominion over him, by what path could it dominate him to make him sin?
Pele Yoetz 137:2: Therefore a man too shall be very zealous to be careful with all the stringencies of Passover and stand guard like a lion at the time of performing the mitzvot, that the mitzvot not be interrupted even for a moment, and that there be no dough residue on the utensils used to make the matzot, and that the matzot not be brought close to the oven and remain there even a moment before the baker removes them, for the heat of the oven leaves some trace of leavening - and let money not be considered worth anything in his eyes compared to the love of the Creator. This is a great principle in all the mitzvot, all the more so, a fortiori, for keeping the laws of Passover according to their halachah, and money shall answer for everything.
Pele Yoetz 137:3: And likewise, on the night of the fourteenth, when he performs the search, he should not go through the house casually, but rather, even though he knows the members of the household have already searched well, he shall act as though they had not searched at all. And he shall perform the search well in the cracks and crevices, and gather the ten pieces of bread that are set out, intending that they correspond to the ten crowns of impurity, and afterward recite the formula of "kol chamira," intending its secret in general, to whatever extent our hands can reach, that it is to remove and nullify the spirit of impurity. And one must say it three times, both by day and by night. And after the nullification, let him say the text of prayers that Rabbi Yehuda Ayash arranged, found in the book "Moreh B'Etzba," and I have copied them here to do a kindness for whoever does not have this book.
Pele Yoetz 137:5: May it be Your will, LORD our God and God of our fathers, that You grant us merit to search out the afflictions of the chambers of the soul in which we have acted foolishly by the counsel of the evil inclination, and grant us merit to repent completely. And You, in Your mercy, shall assist us and help us for the sake of the honor of Your Name, and save us from every hint of prohibition, and especially from the prohibition of chametz even in the smallest amount, this year and every year - Amen, so may it be Your will.
Pele Yoetz 137:6: And during the day, let him himself strive to burn the chametz with extra affection, according to the exiles revealed to us that correspond to the ten crowns of impurity, and let his heart be humbled and let him have thoughts of repentance - perhaps he shall merit to make an impression above and the unclean spirit shall be removed through him. And after the burning, let him say the text of "kol chamira" three times, and afterward say:
Pele Yoetz 137:7: May it be Your will, LORD our God and God of our fathers, that You have mercy on us and save us from the prohibition of chametz even in the smallest amount - us and all the members of our household and all the children of Israel - this year and every year, all the days of our lives. And just as we have removed the chametz from our houses and burned it, so grant us merit to remove the evil inclination from within us always, all the days of our lives, and grant us merit to cleave to the good inclination and to Your Torah, Your fear, and Your love always - we, our offspring, and our offspring's offspring - Amen, so may it be Your will.
Pele Yoetz 137:8: However, in order to remove the spirit of impurity from oneself entirely, searching and removing chametz alone do not suffice, but rather the Kabbalists have written that from thirty days before Passover one must set his heart to walk in the way of the good and fulfill some of the paths of repentance, and then the Holy One, blessed be He, brings forth every night a portion of the souls of Israel from within the husks, all according to a person's deeds and according to his own preparation, until on the night the festival is sanctified, free men stand outside - and this is the aspect of the Exodus from Egypt that occurs every single year, and this is the essence of their saying, "a person is obligated to show himself as though he himself had come out of Egypt" (Pesachim 116b), and this is the essence of our joy over our redemption and over the deliverance of our own soul. But if he did not make preparation beforehand and was not careful with chametz as is proper, what does this joy accomplish for him? It is the natural result that he is not aroused so much and joy does not enter his heart so much, for everything depends on his own deeds, on the merit of his own soul, and on his own preparation.
Pele Yoetz 137:9: And all the more so is it necessary to be aroused to repentance during these thirty days before Passover, for our eyes shall fail with our own expectation - we have awaited the saying of the sages of Israel, who said, "in Nisan they were redeemed and in Nisan they are destined to be redeemed" (Rosh Hashanah 11a[?]). And now, because of our sins, the signs [heralding redemption] have been seen in the land for several hundred years, and we have not been saved. And certainly, as these days draw near, Rachel weeps for her children, and the LORD from on high shall roar and from His holy dwelling shall give forth His voice - roaring mightily over His own habitation - and all the host of on high and the Messiah of our righteousness sit and watch with seven eyes to see if the end of wonders has arrived, for it is time to be gracious to her, for the appointed time has come. Therefore every person is obligated to be aroused and do whatever is in his power to do, and pour out his soul before the LORD day by day and night by night regarding the redemption - perhaps he shall find a time of favor, and God, who hears the prayer of every mouth, shall take counsel and hear the voice of his supplications. And in any case, his prayer and his deeds make an impression and an elevation for the Shechinah of our strength through him, and give peace of mind above, for it is upright in the eyes of the LORD when He sees that there is grief over the breaking of the daughter of His people and over the distress of Heaven, and in the end honor shall come, and he shall merit to see the comfort of Zion and the building of our sanctuary and our splendor, which shall be built speedily in our days - Amen, so may it be Your will.
Pele Yoetz 138:1: Reckoning - Reckoning is a great matter: to reckon the reward of a mitzvah against its loss, and the reward of a transgression against its loss - this is a great principle for all knowledge (as I have written under the entry "Reward") - and to reckon what he has lost by wishing to be overly righteous, so that his reward comes out at his own loss (as I shall write below under the entry "Erech" [value]). And he must manage his affairs with judgment, and sometimes the neglect of Torah is itself its fulfillment. And even regarding matters of this world, reckoning is very good: that he make a reckoning of his business dealings and all his conduct, to see which is the straight path he should choose, and choose and draw near between good and better. And when he has business with his fellow, he shall not give to his fellow nor receive from him except by reckoning, and everything in writing, and he shall not discard any reckoning even if it has already passed, for he does not know what a day may bring - perhaps he shall need it. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, already taught us (Derech Eretz Rabbah 5[?]) that he should suspect every person as a robber and honor them as Rabban Gamliel, so that he be saved from suspicion and from being suspected.
Pele Yoetz 138:2: And let him always remember that he is destined to give a judgment and a reckoning before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He. And the commentators explained that they mean that first they ask a person, for the day of judgment for a transgression he has transgressed, what his judgment shall be, and he gives the judgment. And afterward they ask him to give a reckoning of how many times he transgressed that transgression, and he gives the reckoning - for the practice of the court of righteousness of the Holy One, blessed be He, is not like the practice of the courts of flesh and blood, where if one transgresses several transgressions for which he is liable to death, they execute him for one but do not execute him for two - but in the court of the Holy One, blessed be He, a person is punished for every single time, and for every single transgression he transgressed, and one who transgresses a hundred transgressions or a hundred times is not comparable to one who transgresses a hundred and one. Therefore, even if his inclination has overpowered him and he has sinned greatly, he should not add transgression to his sin and do whatever his heart desires, saying, "what is lost is lost," God forbid - rather, whatever is in his power to do to subdue his inclination so as to have one less transgression, or one fewer time, or to do some good thing, even the smallest amount, even once in a jubilee, let him do it, for everything joins into the reckoning, and when the day of judgment and reckoning arrives, he shall give thanks for not having done more evil and for all the good he did, and he shall regret not having subdued his inclination more, as much as he could have - for God shall bring everything into judgment, and the fruit of his deeds shall be eaten, distress and desolation, in measure, in weight, and in proportion.
Pele Yoetz 139:1: Importance - An obligation rests upon a person to hold the mitzvah important, as they said in the Midrash (Tanchuma, Vayigash, 6): the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "the mitzvot are My messengers - whoever honors My messengers is as though he honors Me." And likewise one must greatly value books and treat them with honor, for they are as precious as the King's garments. And likewise one must value and show honor to every person, and value every kind of favor that any person thinks to do for him - even if, in truth, it is not important to him, he shall show a pleasant countenance as though it were very important to him - this is the straight path. But regarding himself, he should not seek importance and should not care at all if they do not consider him important, and when he finds an opportunity to be exacting about this, and the nearby inclination entices him to seek that they consider him important, let him muster his strength with pure thoughts to reckon what man is, that his blood is vanity, and what does it give him and what does it add for him if men like himself consider him important or despise him? And if a person knew the virtue of one who is despised and lowly among men in this world, how greatly he is exalted in the World to Come, it would be fitting for him to seek and desire that he have no importance at all and be a disgrace among men and despised by the people. And they have already said in the Holy Zohar that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai said, after his death, to Rabbi Elazar his son, "would that you not be mentioned in that world," and the head of the heavenly academy said: whoever is great in that world is small in this world, and whoever is small in that world is great in this world.
Pele Yoetz 139:2: And what shall the son do whom Heaven has favored to be important in the eyes of people? This is his remedy: that he be despised and disgraceful in his own eyes and his heart not envy importance at all - and all the more so should he not be at all exacting if at some time they do not consider him important and do something against his honor, but rather let his heart rejoice and his own honor exult, and through this he shall not lose the honor with which they honor him. And according to the greatness of this trait, which is a branch of the branches of humility, which is greater than all of them, so is its rarity precious - for great is the evil of man on earth, for every inclination of the thoughts of his heart is that they consider him important and honor him, and through this he stumbles into jealousy, desire, and honor, which remove a person from the world (Avot 4:21), and in the end he shall be sated with disgrace instead of honor.
Pele Yoetz 139:3: Whoever desires life shall muster his strength to remove the mask of blindness from before his eyes, and flee from importance and from honor as one flees from fire, for it is a fire that consumes unto destruction, and whoever errs in it is a fool and an ignorant simpleton who does not know that the evil inclination has spread a net for his feet, and thinks that this is part of perfection, to show that he feels it - and people say he does not wish to be considered a boor, for whoever does not feel it is not [fully] a person. If only they were wise, they would understand that it is their own wisdom and understanding to merit abundant good - it is better for a person that they consider him a fool than that he be evil before the Omnipresent, and let him not cause evil to his own soul in this world and the World to Come, but rather he shall live a life of contentment for the World to Come and his honor shall be great - and whoever has a brain in his skull shall understand this, for this is his honor.
